en: PHIVOLCS declares a six-kilometer Permanent Danger Zone around Mayon Volcano to protect people from sudden eruptions.
The 1,250-kilometer Philippine Fault Zone crosses many provinces, so residents living near it must practice earthquake drills regularly.
Baguio City's high elevation gives it a cool climate, so visitors should pack warm jackets to prevent catching a cold.
The Cagayan River is the longest in the Philippines, so swimmers must avoid its strong, unpredictable currents during the rainy season.
Tuguegarao City often records the highest temperatures in the Philippines, so students must drink plenty of water to avoid heatstroke.
Mangrove forests in Palawan act as natural barriers against storm surges, protecting coastal communities from dangerous flooding during typhoons.
Laguna de Bay is the largest lake in the Philippines, but swimming in its polluted areas can cause severe skin infections.
Mt. Pulag's freezing temperatures at its peak can cause hypothermia, so hikers must bring thick jackets and avoid heavy rain.
Taal Volcano's fine ash can irritate your lungs and eyes, so residents nearby should wear masks and goggles during eruptions.
Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park has strong underwater currents, so snorkelers must always wear life vests and stay with their guides.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River has dark, slippery caves, so visitors must wear helmets and use flashlights to avoid falling.
Water from mountain springs near Mt. Makiling must be boiled before drinking to kill harmful bacteria and prevent stomach illnesses.
